newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Petrobras expects to keep proven oil reserves.
newsitem.headline: Petrobras expects to keep proven oil reserves.

text.p: Brazil's federally-owned oil firm Petrobras expects to keep control of the country's proven oil reserves after a new oil law is approved by Congress, said a company official.

"We believe that the 8.0 billion barrels in proven oil reserves will remain under Petrobras' control after the new oil law is approved," Hernani Fortuna, chief of the company's Financial Planning division, told reporters.
Brazilian oil and gas reserves totalled 14 billion barrels at the end of 1996, of which 8.0 billion barrels were proven oil reserves.
According to a draft version of the bill presented to Congress, Petrobras will be allowed to maintain areas where it is already producing or involved in exploration work.
It gives the firm three months after approval of the new law to inform which areas it wants to keep.

The new oil law is aimed at regulating the opening up of Brazil's oil and gas industries to private investment. The Brazilian Congress voted in 1995 to end the state's monopoly on oil and gas but has not yet approved the enabling legislation to put that decision into practice.

Fortuna, speaking at a conference on Latin American utilities sponsored by Caspian Securities, said Petrobras aims to increase its oil output to 1.5 million barrels per day in the year 2000. The company ended last year with a daily average production of slightly over 800,000 barrels.

Petrobras' recent oil discovery, with potential reserves of 1.3 billion barrels, will help the company increase its production in coming years. The firm plans to start producing 150,000 barrels per day in the offshore oil field Roncador in 1999, Fortuna said.
The discovery, announced last December, was made 1,853 metres below water level of the Campos Basin, just off the coast of Rio de Janeiro.

Fortuna also said Petrobras invested $3.07 billion last year, of which 33 percent were invested in development and research, 23 percent in exploration, 21 percent in refining, 12 percent in terminals and pipelines, 1.0 percent in shipping and 10 percent in others.
In coming years Petrobras plans to increase investments in refining to improve the capacity of its refineries.
"We need to invest to adapt our refineries to the oil we are now producing," Fortuna said, adding that Petrobras plans to increase its refining capacity to 1.7 million barrels per day by 1999.
Petrobras ranked the world's 21st company in oil production and the ninth in refining at the end of 1996, Fortuna said.
According to a study by Caspian Securities, Brazil is likely to be the fourth largest oil producer in the next four years, after Iraq, Venezuela and Colombia.
